digest.definition: The study of the whole human past, from human origins to recent events, tracing change and continuity across society, politics, economics, culture, ideas and environments
distinctiveFeatures: The study of the whole human past, from human origins to recent events, tracing change and continuity across society, politics, economics, culture, ideas and environments
Allied to the humanities, arts and social sciences, yet distinct in its sense of the past, its respect for context and its rigorous handling of evidence
No fixed canon: historians recognise no required body of knowledge or core, so courses legitimately differ in content, teaching and assessment

Six central features: depth of time; geographical range and comparison; close work on primary sources; critical, historiographical and ethical awareness; varied specialisms; an extended independent piece of work
A non-sequential subject: progression is cumulative and qualitative rather than a fixed order of modules
Multi-perspectival and, by its own account, uncomfortable, attending to non-dominant and marginalised cultures

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: the subject recovers the diversity of past experience and is multi-perspectival; it faces uncomfortable pasts, attends to marginalised cultures and commits its community to widening participation, inclusive curricula and decolonising the curriculum (D1, 1.12 to 1.14); teaching methods should be inclusive (D1, 3.7)

courses aim to be highly accessible through varied teaching and assessment, digital resources and attention to students facing practical barriers: disability, health conditions, caring, commuting, low income and religious observance (D1, 2.2); flexible and part-time delivery follow (D1, 2.8)

headed Sustainability: content and method serve the UN goals, with environmental, public, economic and cultural history to the fore, links to heritage and conservation, and a mindset of change, continuity and causation (D1, 1.16 to 1.18); a generic skill and teaching methods carry it (D1, 4.6, 3.7)

headed Entrepreneurship and enterprise education: employability built into modules through real-world tasks such as policy papers, group work and presentations; career resilience; a wide spread of graduate careers (D1, 1.19 to 1.21)

subjectSpecific.text: By the end of your degree, you should be able to frame pertinent, well-reasoned and tightly focused questions about the past.
By the end of your degree, you should be able to find out where trustworthy, exact knowledge about the past is held and how to reach it.

By the end of your degree, you should be able to plan and carry out a structured enquiry, from setting your own tasks to collecting, filtering, ordering, combining and analysing large bodies of primary and secondary evidence.
By the end of your degree, you should be able to draw on sound, pertinent evidence and argument.
By the end of your degree, you should be able to handle references, reading lists and bibliographies well.

By the end of your degree, you should be able to analyse claims, recognising that some statements are better founded than others, and that historians test claims by rules of evidence which are themselves open to critique and which belong to intellectual integrity more widely.

By the end of your degree, you should be able to analyse primary sources critically and with empathy, asking about their genre, content, viewpoint and purpose, taking primary sources to mean any textual, visual, material or oral evidence from the past that is being examined.

By the end of your degree, you should be able to grasp the problems of the historical record: weighing differing viewpoints, interpreting material that is complex, unclear, contradictory or partial, and seeing where knowledge stops and where over-simple explanation misleads, a grasp that also helps them test historical claims made in public life.

By the end of your degree, you should be able to appreciate how varied and complicated past situations, events and outlooks were, and so how varied the present is, seeing history as a subject that resists reduction and builds intellectual maturity.

By the end of your degree, you should be able to understand how people lived, acted and thought in past settings that always differ from our own, meeting the strangeness of the past, coming to understand unfamiliar structures, cultures and beliefs, and so gaining empathy and respect for difference.
By the end of your degree, you should be able to hold to a reasoned argument when others disagree, listen, debate at length and change your view where evidence and argument call for it.
By the end of your degree, you should be able to build an argument around questions about the past that matter, and that also bear on the present and future.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a History degree

statements.appliesTo: students of History
statements.about: handling information and arguing for audiences, for employability
statements.paraphrase: Because the subject works across a wide range of sources, History students must become skilled at finding, choosing, interpreting, analysing and combining information from large analogue and digital datasets, and at condensing complex knowledge into clear, reasoned arguments for varied audiences.

forPractitioner.text: Because historical work spans many kinds of source, students must become adept at retrieving, selecting, interpreting, analysing and combining information from large paper and digital collections, and at turning complex knowledge into clear, reasoned arguments for different audiences.

forBeneficiary.text: Because history draws on so many kinds of source, you must become skilled at finding, sorting, interpreting and combining information from large paper and digital collections, and at turning complex material into clear, reasoned arguments for different audiences.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a History degree

statements.appliesTo: History courses focused mainly on one country
statements.about: comparison in courses centred on one country
statements.paraphrase: A course centred mainly on one country brings in sustained, serious comparison with other places and should take several perspectives.

forPractitioner.text: Where one country dominates a course, build in serious, sustained comparison with others: the course should take more than one perspective.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on course design; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Distinctive features of a History degree

statements.appliesTo: History honours courses and their students
statements.about: close work on primary sources from the period
statements.paraphrase: Close study of material produced in the period being studied is indispensable to the degree.

forPractitioner.text: Give every student the chance to study closely source material from the period being taught; the statement calls this essential.

forBeneficiary.text: You will get the chance to work closely with sources created in the period you are studying, a central part of learning history.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a History degree

statements.appliesTo: students of History
statements.about: historiographical, methodological and ethical awareness across modules
statements.paraphrase: Students are expected to show awareness and understanding of historiography and method in every module and in long independent work, to receive guidance in research ethics and show they apply it, and to know the subject's conventions for quoting and reproducing others' work.

forPractitioner.text: Expect students to show historiographical and methodological awareness in all modules and in extended independent work; give them guidance in research ethics that they can show they apply, including institutional and archive codes, and teach the conventions for quoting and reproducing others' work.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to show that you understand how historians have written about your topics and the methods they use, in every module and in longer independent work, to apply research ethics, including any archive or university codes, and to follow the subject's rules on quoting others.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a History degree

statements.appliesTo: History departments
statements.about: explaining progression in a non-sequential subject
statements.paraphrase: History has no fixed order of modules, so departments carry the responsibility to explain clearly how each course supports progression across its years.

forPractitioner.text: Because the subject is not sequential, set out clearly in course documents how the course builds progression year on year; the statement makes this the department's responsibility.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a responsibility of the department in course design; the student sees its effect in course documents

headingPath: Distinctive features of a History degree

statements.appliesTo: students and graduates of History honours courses
statements.about: yearly attainment towards the threshold; readiness for postgraduate study
statements.paraphrase: Each year is expected to bring knowledge, expertise and experience that build towards meeting every threshold subject and generic skill in the statement; a graduate with a second-class degree or better is expected to be ready for postgraduate study in History or a related field.

forPractitioner.text: Plan each year so that attainment builds towards all the threshold subject-specific and generic skills by graduation; a graduate with at least a second-class degree is expected to be ready and able to take on postgraduate study.

forBeneficiary.text: Each year of your degree is meant to build your knowledge and skills towards the full set of minimum outcomes; if you graduate with a second-class degree or higher, you are expected to be ready for postgraduate study in history or a related subject.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a History degree

statements.appliesTo: joint honours undergraduates
statements.about: joint honours: part of the subject and generic skills
statements.paraphrase: Joint honours students will reach some of the subject's specific and generic skills and will gain others from the other subjects they study.

forPractitioner.text: In joint honours, graduates will meet some of History's subject-specific and generic skills and will add others from the partner subjects; design the History part with that in mind.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study History jointly with another subject, you will develop some of the history skills and add others from your other subject.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a History degree

statements.appliesTo: higher education providers in periodic review
statements.paraphrase: Providers will bring external reviewers into periodic review for an outside view of proposed changes and to make sure threshold standards are met and content suits the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Periodic review will draw on external reviewers for an outside perspective on proposed changes, to confirm that threshold standards are achieved and that content fits the subject.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider's quality assurance

statements.appliesTo: History departments and teaching staff
statements.paraphrase: Teaching and learning methods should also show the need for an inclusive environment and serve the aims of education for sustainable development.

forPractitioner.text: Choose teaching methods that should create an inclusive environment for learning and serve the aims of education for sustainable development.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on teaching design; the student meets its effect

statements.appliesTo: History courses
statements.about: diverse assessment so every student can show their abilities
statements.paraphrase: Assessment needs variety, because no single mode reveals all of a student's abilities and students arrive with different backgrounds; courses should give everyone chances to demonstrate their knowledge, understanding and skills, rewarding strengths while building weaker areas.

forPractitioner.text: Use a variety of assessment modes: no one mode shows the full range of ability, and students arrive with different qualifications, so the course should give all of them chances to demonstrate their knowledge, understanding and abilities.
